title: Rise and fall
hookLine: Ibn Khaldun saw that unity builds and comfort loosens

lines: A NEW STRETCH: WHAT THE HISTORY TEACHES.
cards: A scholar is lowered down a city wall on ropes to talk with a conqueror. We've met him before, and today he opens a new stretch with a different question.

For a long time this path has walked through history: cities founded, caliphs crowned, libraries filled, armies at the gates, dynasties that came in from the desert and faded out in palaces. Names, places, reigns.
Now step back from the map. What does all of it teach? Not about kings.
About people, and a faith carried through time. Today: rise and fall.

teach.b: Ibn Khaldun, the historian of Tunis, looked at the dynasties of North Africa and saw a pattern. A group bound tightly together, by kinship, hardship and loyalty, gains the strength to build.
Then comfort settles in, the next generations inherit power without the struggle that made it, and the bond loosens. He called that bond asabiyya.
We met the idea earlier this year; today, hold it up against everything since. A movement rises from the Sahara or the mountains, sure of itself and of each other, and builds.
A court grows splendid, and its rivals grow inside the walls. Ibn Khaldun wrote of it almost like a life span, as natural to dynasties as age is to a person. He didn't call it a punishment.
Read today, it works as a warning. Second, the Qur'an names the bond in its own way.

teach.h: HOLD FAST TO THE ROPE TOGETHER.
teach.b: In Pickthall's translation: "And hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate." A rope, gripped by many hands at once. Let go one by one, and nobody notices at first.
Third, a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari pictures believers as a building, each part holding up the others, and the Prophet, peace be upon him, laced his fingers together to show it.

teach.h: FAMILIES AND TEAMS RISE AND DRIFT TOO.

teach.b: A family, a mosque, a group of friends, a team at work: each rises when people show up for one another, and drifts when everyone gets comfortable enough not to. Comfort isn't a sin; nobody is told to live in a tent.
But bonds that aren't tended loosen on their own.

how: Muslims often speak of the community as one body or one building, and gather for congregational prayer, Friday prayer, family visits and the Eids partly to keep those bonds strong.

o: the bond of loyalty that lets a group build
the comfort that slowly weakens a dynasty
the rope of God that believers hold fast

games.q: rise and fall — tap the pairs.
p: the bond that holds a group together
historian of Tunis who saw the pattern

s: Ibn Khaldun said comfort is a sin
he described a pattern, almost a life span: comfort loosens the bond that built a people. a description, not a ruling.
the Qur'an pictures unity as a rope held by many hands
"and hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate."
the pattern only applies to empires
the same rise and drift can happen in a family, a mosque or a team.

games.q: your mosque was built by a small group who carried every chair themselves. years later it's comfortable, and fewer people show up to help. what does Ibn Khaldun's pattern suggest?
o: nothing; comfort means the job is done.
the bond that built it needs tending, or it will loosen.
go back to carrying chairs forever.
games.why: his pattern says the bond that builds weakens once comfort comes and the struggle is forgotten; the Qur'an's image is holding the rope together.

practice: Lace your fingers together the way the Prophet did, and feel how each hand holds the other.

Then think of one bond that has gone slack, a cousin you only see at weddings, a friend from an old job, a neighbor whose name you never learned, and choose one small thing that would pull the rope a little tighter.
Hold that person in mind for a while.

wordCard.voice: Asabiyya, the bond of kinship, hardship and loyalty that Ibn Khaldun said builds a people up before comfort loosens it. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: rope, cord. the Qur'an's image (3:103) for holding together.

carryVoice: Your line: unity builds. Comfort loosens the bonds that nobody tends. That's today, done.

sources.ref: Ibn Khaldun, al-Muqaddimah (on asabiyya and the decline of dynasties)
